The foundational concept of ordinate sets—both lower V\(f) and upper V(f)—is central to the development of product measures and measurable functions. These sets are defined as subsets of the product space X × R, where X is a measurable space and R is the reals. For a non-negative function f, the lower ordinate set V\(f) consists of points (x, t) such that 0 ≤ t ≤ f(x), while the upper ordinate set V(f) includes (x, t) with f(x) ≤ t ≤ ∞. The measurability of these sets is established through key propositions: (5a) for simple functions, (5d) for measurable functions, and (5c) for monotone sequences. The interplay between these sets under inclusion and limit operations provides a dual structure essential for integration theory. In GSI, this duality supports Bayesian inference by enabling probabilistic interpretations of measurable functions. In GSE, it underpins state transitions through measurable mappings of ordinate sets. The failure mode arises when f lacks measurability or when sequences do not converge properly, disrupting the σ-algebraic closure required for consistent measure-theoretic operations.
